wobble.e: From earlier wabble (“wobble”), probably from Low German wabbeln (“to wobble”).

woe.e: From Middle English wo, woo, from Old English wā, wǣ, from Proto-West Germanic *wai (interjection), from Proto-Germanic *wai (“woe!”, interjection), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wáy (“oh!; ah!; woe!; alas!”, interjection).
woe.g: Great sadness or distress; a misfortune causing such sadness.

woeful.e: From Middle English woful, waful, equivalent to woe + -ful.
woeful.g: Full of woe; sorrowful; distressed with grief or calamity.

woke.e: Shortened from woken or woken up, or derived from dialectal use of woke (past participle of wake). The sense of being aware of social injustice dates to at least the 1930s. The derogatory use has been most commonly used as of the 2020s.

wolf.e: From Middle English wolf, from Old English wulf, ƿulf, from Proto-West Germanic *wulf, from Proto-Germanic *wulfaz, from Proto-Indo-European *wĺ̥kʷos.
wolf.g: Canis lupus; the largest wild member of the canine subfamily.

woman.e: From Middle English womman, from earlier wimman, wifman, from Old English wīfmann (“woman”, literally “female person”), a compound of wīf (“woman, female”, whence English wife) + mann (“person, human being”, whence English man). For details on the pronunciation and spelling history, see the usage notes below.

womankind.e: From Middle English wommankynde. By surface analysis, woman + -kind.

womb.e: From Middle English wombe, wambe, from Old English womb, wamb (“belly, stomach; bowels; heart; womb; hollow”), from Proto-West Germanic *wambu, from Proto-Germanic *wambō (“belly, stomach, abdomen”).
womb.g: In female mammals, the organ in which the young are conceived and grow until birth; the uterus.

women.e: From Middle English wimmen, from Old English wīfmenn (“women”), from wīf (“female”) + menn (“men, persons, human beings”), equivalent to wife + men. Spelling (with o) influenced by the singular; see woman for more.

won.e: Past participle of win, from Old English winnan.

won't.e: From earlier wonnot, from Middle English wynnot, wilnot, wolnot, wilnat, a contraction of Middle English will not, wil not, wyll not, will noght, wil noht, willi noȝt, wyl nat, wol not, woll not, wole not, wolle not, wol nat, woll nat, etc., equivalent to a will + not and/or woll + not. For the pronunciation with /oʊ/, /əʊ/, see poultry.
won't.g: will not (negative auxiliary); used to indicate a future non-occurring action.

wonder.e: From Middle English wonder, wunder, from Old English wundor (“wonder, miracle, marvel”), from Proto-West Germanic *wundr, from Proto-Germanic *wundrą. Via PIE cognate with English wish (see more).
wonder.g: A sense of awe, astonishment and curiosity, inspired by unexpected events, novel experiences and inexplicable circumstances, sometimes accom

wonderful.e: From Middle English wonderful, wondirful, from Old English wundorful (“wonderful”), from Proto-West Germanic *wundrafull, equivalent to wonder + -ful.
wonderful.g: Tending to excite wonder; surprising, extraordinary.

wonderfully.e: From Middle English wonderfully, wunderfullie, wonderfulliche, equivalent to wonderful + -ly.

wondrous.e: From Middle English wondrous, alteration after the suffix -ous of Middle English wonders (“wondrous, wonderful”, adjective), from Old English wundres (“of wonder”), genitive singular of wundor (“wonder, miracle”), from Proto-Germanic *wundrą (“wonder”).

wont.e: From Middle English wont, from Old English ġewunod, past participle of ġewunian (“to be accustomed to, dwell”), the noun sense possibly arising via conflation of wone (“custom, habit, practice”) and the adjective wont. Likely related to wone, wonder, wean, and win.
wont.g: One's habitual way of doing things; custom, habit, practice.

wont.e: From Middle English wonten (“to accustom”), from wont (adjective).
wont.g: To make (someone) used to; to accustom.

wood.e: From Middle English wode, from Old English wudu, widu (“wood, forest, grove; tree; timber”), from Proto-West Germanic *widu, from Proto-Germanic *widuz (“wood”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁weydʰh₁- (“to separate”). The spelling developed as it did in wool.
wood.g: The substance making up the central part of the trunk and branches of a tree. Used as a material for construction, to manufacture various it

wood.e: From Middle English wood, from Old English wōd (“mad, insane”).

woodcutter.g: A person who cuts down trees, especially as an occupation; a lumberjack.

wooded.e: From Middle English woded (“concealed by trees”), equivalent to wood + -ed.

wooden.e: From wood + -en. Dates from 1530s, gradually replaced treen (“made from a tree”), from Middle English treen, from Old English triewen.

woodland.e: From Middle English wodeland, wodelond, from Old English wuduland (“woodland; forestland; forest”), equivalent to wood + land. Eclipsed non-native Middle English salt (“woodland”), borrowed from Latin saltus (“woodland, forest”).
woodland.g: Of a creature or object: growing, living, or existing in a woodland.

woodpile.g: A pile of cut wood to be used as fuel.

woodwork.e: From Middle English woodewerk (“carpentry”), equivalent to wood + work.
woodwork.g: Something made from wood, especially cabinets and trim (e.g., baseboards, doorframes) made from millwork.

woof.e: The interjection and noun are onomatopoeic. Interjection etymology 2, interjection sense 2 (“used to express strong physical attraction for someone”) probably alludes to the eager barking of a dog.
woof.g: Used to indicate the sound of a dog barking, or something resembling it.

woof.e: From WWOOF, an acronym of World Wide Opportunities on Organic Farms which is a network of national organizations that facilitate homestays on organic farms.

wool.e: From Middle English wolle, from Old English wull, from Proto-West Germanic *wullu, from Proto-Germanic *wullō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wĺ̥h₁neh₂. The vowel development u → o → oo is purely graphical.
wool.g: The hair of the sheep, llama and some other ruminants.

word.e: From Middle English word, from Old English word, from Proto-West Germanic *word, from Proto-Germanic *wurdą (“word”), from Proto-Indo-European *werdʰom (“word”), from *werh₁- (“to say, speak”).
word.g: The smallest unit of language that has a particular meaning and can be expressed by itself; the smallest discrete, meaningful unit of langua

word.e: Variant of worth (“to become, turn into, grow, get”), from Middle English worthen, from Old English weorþan (“to turn into, become, grow”), from Proto-West Germanic *werþan, from Proto-Germanic *werþaną (“to turn, turn into, become”).

work.e: From Middle English work, werk, from Old English weorc, from Proto-West Germanic *werk, from Proto-Germanic *werką (“work”), from Proto-Indo-European *wérǵom (“work”), from Proto-Indo-European *werǵ- (“to make”).

From Middle English werken and worchen, from Old English wyrċan and wircan (Mercian), from Proto-Germanic *wurkijaną (“to work”), from Proto-Indo-European *wr̥ǵyéti (“to be working, to be at work”), from the root *werǵ-.
work.g: To do a specific task by employing physical or mental powers.

worker.e: From Middle English worchere, werkere, equivalent to work + -er.
worker.g: One who works: a person who performs labor for a living; traditionally, especially, manual labor.

working.e: From Middle English workyng, wirkynge, worchinge, werchinge, workinde, wirkand, worchende, wurchende, from Old English wyrċende, from Proto-Germanic *wurkijandz, present participle of Proto-Germanic *wurkijaną (“to work”), equivalent to work + -ing.

workload.g: The amount of work assigned to a particular worker, normally in a specified time period.

workman.e: From Middle English werkman, from Old English weorcmann (“workman”), from Proto-West Germanic *werkamann, from Proto-Germanic *werkamann- (“workman”), equivalent to work + -man.
workman.g: A man who labours for wages.

workmanship.e: From Middle English werkmanschipe, equivalent to workman + -ship.
workmanship.g: The skill of an artisan or craftsman.

world.e: From Middle English world, from Old English weorold (“world”), from Proto-West Germanic *weraldi, from Proto-Germanic *weraldiz (“lifetime, human existence, world”, literally “age/era of man”), equivalent to wer (“man”) + eld (“age”). Eclipsed non-native Middle English mounde (“world”), from Old French monde, munde (“world”).
world.g: The subjective human experience, regarded collectively; human collective existence; existence in general; the reality we live in.

worldly.e: From Middle English worldly, worldlich, wordly (adjective), from Old English woruldlīċ, worldlīċ, weoroldlīċ (“worldly; earthly; temporal; mundane; secular”), from Proto-Germanic *weraldilīkaz, equivalent to world + -ly.
worldly.g: Concerned with human or earthly matters, physical as opposed to spiritual.

worldly.e: From Middle English worldly, worldliche, wordly (adverb), from Old English woroldlīċe, weoroldlīċe; equivalent to world + -ly (adverbial suffix).

worm.e: From Middle English werm, wirm, worm, worme, wrim, wurm, wyrm, wyrme, from Old English weorm, wurm, wyrm, from Proto-West Germanic *wurmi, from Proto-Germanic *wurmiz (“worm; snake”), from Proto-Indo-European *wr̥mis (“worm; larva”), possibly from *wer- (“to turn”).
worm.g: A generally tubular invertebrate of the annelid phylum; an earthworm.

wormwood.e: From Middle English wormwode, a folk etymology (as if worm + wood) of wermode (“wormwood”), from Old English wermōd (“wormwood, absinthe”), from Proto-West Germanic *warjamōdā (“wormwood”).
wormwood.g: An intensely bitter herb (Artemisia absinthium and similar plants in genus Artemisia) used in medicine, in the production of absinthe and ve

worn.e: By analogy to past participles like torn from tear and sworn from swear.
worn.g: Damaged and shabby as a result of much use.

worn-out.e: From worn (adjective; and past participle of wear) + out.
worn-out.g: Damaged due to continued or hard exposure or use until no longer effective or useful.

worry.e: From Middle English worien (“to choke, strangle”), from Old English wyrġan, from Proto-West Germanic *wurgijan, from Proto-Germanic *wurgijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *werǵʰ- (“bind, squeeze”).
worry.g: To be troubled; to give way to mental anxiety or doubt.

worrying.e: From Middle English werying, equivalent to worry + -ing.
worrying.g: The act of worrying or harassing somebody.

worse.e: From Middle English worse, werse, from Old English wiersa, from Proto-West Germanic *wirsiʀō, from Proto-Germanic *wirsizô.

worship.e: From Middle English worschipe /worthschipe, inherited from Old English weorþsċiepe. By surface analysis, wor(th) + -ship.
worship.g: The devotion accorded to a deity or to a sacred object.

worshipper.e: From Middle English wirshiper, worchyppar, worscheper, worschepour, worschiper, worschippar, worshipore; equivalent to worship + -er.
worshipper.g: A person who worships, especially at a place of assembly for religious services.

worst.e: From Middle English worste, wurste, warste, werste, wirste, from Old English wierrest, from Proto-Germanic *wirsistaz, superlative form of *ubilaz (“bad, evil”); compare worse.
worst.g: superlative form of bad: most bad

worth.e: From Middle English worth, from Old English weorþ, from Proto-West Germanic *werþ, from Proto-Germanic *werþaz (“worthy, valuable”); from Proto-Indo-European *wert-.
worth.g: Having a value of; proper to be exchanged for.

worth.e: From Middle English worthen, wurthen, werthen (“to be; exist; come into being; come into existence”), from Old English weorþan (“to come into being; be made; become; arise; be”), from Proto-West Germanic *werþan, from Proto-Germanic *werþaną (“to come about; happen; come into being; become”), from Proto-Indo-European *wert- (“to turn; turn out”).

worthily.e: From Middle English worthely, worthili, worthiliche, worthily, worthyly, worþili, worþiliche, worþily, wurðelice, wurðeliche, wurðelike, wurthelie, wurthilyche, wurthyly, equivalent to worthy + -ly.

worthless.e: From Middle English *worthles, from Old English weorþlēas (“worthless”), equivalent to worth + -less.
worthless.g: Having no worth or use; without value.

worthwhile.g: Good and important enough to spend time, effort, or money on.

worthy.e: From Middle English worthy, wurthi, from Old English *weorþiġ (“worthy”), equivalent to worth + -y.

From Middle English worthien, wurthien, from Old English weorþian (“to esteem, honor, worship, distinguish, celebrate, exalt, praise, adorn, deck, enrich, reward”), from Proto-Germanic *werþōną (“to be worthy, estimate, appreciate, appraise”), from Proto-Indo-European *wert- (“to turn, wind”).
worthy.g: To render or treat as worthy.

wot.e: From wit, in return from Old English witan.

wound.e: Noun from Middle English wund, from Old English wund, from Proto-West Germanic *wundu, from Proto-Germanic *wundō (“wound”), from Proto-Indo-European *wen- (“to strive, toil, win”). Verb from Middle English wunden, from Old English wundian, from Proto-Germanic *wundōną (“to wound”).
wound.g: An injury, such as a cut, stab, or tear, to a (usually external) part of the body.

wear.e: From Middle English weren, from Old English werian (“to clothe, cover over; put on, wear, use; stock (land)”), from Proto-West Germanic *waʀjan, from Proto-Germanic *wazjaną (“to clothe”), from Proto-Indo-European *wes- (“to dress, put on (clothes)”). Originally a weak verb (i.e.

From Middle English weren, werien, from Old English werian (“to guard, keep, defend; ward off, hinder, prevent, forbid; restrain; occupy, inhabit; dam up; discharge obligations on (land)”), from Proto-West Germanic *warjan, from Proto-Germanic *warjaną (“to defend, protect, ward off”).
wear.g: To guard; watch; keep watch, especially from entry or invasion.

weave.e: From Middle English weven (“to weave”), from Old English wefan (“to weave”), from Proto-West Germanic *weban, from Proto-Germanic *webaną, from Proto-Indo-European *webʰ- (“to weave, braid”).
weave.g: To form something by passing lengths or strands of material over and under one another.

weave.e: From Middle English weven (“to wander”); probably from Old Norse veifa (“move around, wave”), related to Latin vibrare.
weave.g: To move by turning and twisting.
